entities.summary:
The Carolingian dynasty (751–987 CE) was a Frankish royal house that produced Charlemagne (Charles the Great), who united most of Western Europe under one rule for the first time since the fall of Rome. The dynasty's cultural, religious, and administrative innovations created the foundations of medieval European civilization and the concept of a Christian Europe unified under church and empire.

Charlemagne (r.768-814 CE) conquered the Saxons, Lombards, and Avars, creating an empire spanning modern France, Germany, Italy, and neighboring territories. His coronation as Holy Roman Emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800 CE established the principle of papal authority to crown secular rulers — a relationship that dominated European politics for 700 years. The Carolingian Renaissance, promoted by Charlemagne at his court in Aachen, standardized Latin script, promoted literacy, and preserved classical manuscripts in monastery scriptoria.

The 843 Treaty of Verdun, dividing Charlemagne's empire among his three grandsons, created the territorial outlines of modern France and Germany — making it arguably the founding document of Western European nationhood. Charlemagne's administrative innovations (missi dominici, county system, standardized weights and measures) created governance templates that persisted through the High Middle Ages.
